problems.title: Chain versus tree
problems.solution: A chain needs 1,023 dependent steps. A tree needs $\log_2 1024 = 10$ rounds and still $512 + 256 + \dots + 1 = 1023$ additions: same work, much shorter critical path.

problems.title: Counting warp-rounds
problems.statement: A 256-thread block reduces 256 values in shared memory over 8 rounds. Count, summed over rounds, the warps that have at least one active thread (each such warp issues the round's instructions).

parts.prompt: Interleaved addressing (round r: threads with t mod 2^{r+1} = 0)?

hints: Interleaved: count the warps holding a multiple of 2, 4, 8, …
Sequential: 128, 64, 32 active threads, then within one warp.
problems.solution: (a) Per round: [8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 4, 2, 1], total 47. (b) Per round: [4, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1], total 12. Sequential addressing issues 3.9× fewer warp-rounds, with no divergence until the last warp, and no bank conflicts.

problems.title: Interleaved, one round
problems.statement: 256-thread block, interleaved addressing, the round where threads with $t \bmod 4 = 0$ work.

parts.prompt: Lane efficiency of those warps, in %?

problems.solution: 64 threads spread over all 8 warps, 8 per warp: every warp issues at 25% efficiency. Sequential addressing would put the same 64 threads in 2 full warps.

problems.title: Shuffle trees

parts.prompt: After those steps, which lanes hold the full sum?
To leave the sum in every lane instead, use…

hints: With shfl_down, lane ℓ adds lane ℓ + d; lanes near the top read nothing new.
problems.solution: 5 steps. With shfl_down only lane 0 accumulates everything (upper lanes receive their own or stale values). With shfl_xor each step exchanges symmetrically, so after 5 steps every lane has the total, which saves a broadcast when every thread needs the result (softmax, LayerNorm).

problems.title: Sizing a reduction
problems.statement: Reduce $n = 2^{26}$ floats on the GW-1 with a full machine: 128 blocks of 256 threads, a grid-stride loop, then one partial per block.

parts.prompt: Fraction of all additions done in the shuffle/shared-memory trees, in %?

hints: Tree additions: 255 per block, plus 127 to combine the partials.
problems.solution: (a) 2,048. (b) 128. (c) About $(128 \times 255 + 127)/2^{26} \approx 0.049\%$. The tree, with all its barriers and shuffles, is a rounding error; the grid-stride loop is the kernel.

problems.title: Is it fast?
problems.statement: Reducing $2^{26}$ floats takes 0.60 ms on the GW-1.
problems.solution: (a) 256 MiB at 512 GB/s: 0.524 ms. (b) 87%: at the practical ceiling.

problems.title: When floats stop counting
problems.statement: Add $2^{25}$ ones in FP32 (round to nearest even).
hints: In a tree, every partial sum is a power of two.
problems.solution: (a) FP32 has 24 bits of significand: $2^{24} + 1$ isn't representable and rounds (to even) back to $2^{24}$, so the loop sticks at 16,777,216. (b) The tree adds equal powers of two at every level, all exact: 33,554,432. Trees aren't only faster; their error grows like $\log n$ instead of $n$.

problems.title: Combining blocks
problems.statement: How do you combine per-block partial sums?

parts.prompt: Which of these give bit-identical float results on every run?
options: A second kernel summing the partials in a fixed order
Each block atomicAdd-ing its partial into the result
The last-block-done pattern, where the last block sums the partials in index order
Each block atomicAdd-ing into one of 8 accumulators chosen by blockIdx % 8, then summing the 8

hints: Does the order of additions depend on timing?
problems.solution: Fixed-order sums of the partials are deterministic. Float atomics add in arrival order, which varies, so they aren't, even when spread over several accumulators (Lab 9 measures this).

problems.title: Work, span and Brent
problems.statement: Reduction of $n = 2^{20}$ values with $p = 32{,}768$ processors (threads). Brent's bound: $T_p \le W/p + S$, where W is total work and S the span (longest dependent chain).

parts.prompt: Brent's bound on T_p, in steps?

problems.solution: (a) $n - 1$. (b) $\log_2 n = 20$. (c) $\approx 32 + 20 = 52$ steps, against $10^6$ sequentially. With $p \ll n$ the work term dominates, which is why each thread should first add many elements sequentially: it doesn't increase W and keeps the tree small.

problems.title: A dot product
problems.statement: Fused dot product of two FP32 vectors of $2^{26}$ elements on the GW-1.

parts.prompt: Lower bound on time, in ms?

hints: Two reads and two FLOPs per element.
problems.solution: (a) 0.25. (b) 512 MiB / 512 GB/s = 1.049 ms. The reduction tree is free; fusing the multiply into the reduction (instead of writing products and then summing them) saves a third of the traffic.
